knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination of Simplex in the Nondegenerate Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-termination and terminal-outcome theorem for a feasible standard-form minimization LP whose basic feasible solutions are all nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the feasible set is nonempty and every basic feasible solution is nondegenerate. Then the simplex method terminates after finitely many iterations. At termination, either it has an optimal basis \(B\) and an associated optimal basic feasible solution, or it has found \(d\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\geq0\), and \(c^Td<0\), in which case the optimal value is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the LP is feasible and every basic feasible solution is nondegenerate, simplex terminates finitely. It returns either an optimal basis and basic feasible solution or a nonnegative recession direction of negative cost proving that the problem is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \{x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\ne\varnothing
\forall x\in\operatorname{BFS}(P),\quad x\text{ is nondegenerate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Simplex terminates finitely, and either returns an optimal basis and associated basic feasible solution, or returns }d\text{ with }Ad=0,\ d\geq0,\ c^Td<0\text{ and }\inf c^Tx=-\infty.

children.title: Strict-Improvement Progress
children.top_down_role: Navigation for the objective-progress component of the classical finiteness argument.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\).
The basic solution is nondegenerate: \(x_B=B^{-1}b>0\).
An entering index \(j\notin B\) satisfies \(\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}a_j<0\), and the ratio test has a leaving candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{+}<c^{\mathsf T}x\).

notation.meaning: Current basis matrix and basic vector.
Reduced cost of the entering variable.
Primal step length from the ratio test.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate primal simplex progress for a minimization problem in equality standard form.

source_refs.locator: Part 1. Basic Theory: The Simplex Method and Duality p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=B^{-1}a_j\) and \(\theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_B)_i/d_i\). Nondegeneracy gives \(\theta>0\). The adjacent basic feasible solution produced by the pivot satisfies \(x_j^{+}=\theta\), \(x_B^{+}=x_B-\theta d\), and \[c^{\mathsf T}x^{+}-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta\bar c_j<0.\] Thus every feasible improving pivot strictly decreases the objective, so no basic feasible solution with the same objective value can recur along such a pivot sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nondegenerate feasible basis, every improving simplex pivot has positive length and strictly improves the objective.

children.title: Finite Basis-State Space
children.top_down_role: Navigation for the combinatorial-state component of the classical finiteness argument.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
Every pivoted state is identified by its set of \(m\) basic column indices.
The pivot sequence never revisits a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}\le N_{\mathrm{fb}}-1\le \binom{n}{m}-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial finiteness bound for basis-indexed simplex trajectories.

source_refs.locator: Part 1. Basic Theory: The Simplex Method and Duality p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A basis is an \(m\)-element subset \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for which \(A_I\) is nonsingular. Hence there are at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) bases and at most that many primal-feasible bases. A simplex trajectory that starts at one feasible basis and never repeats a basis can therefore perform at most \(N_{\mathrm{fb}}-1\) pivots. In particular, strict objective improvement at every pivot prevents recurrence and yields finite termination, although this combinatorial bound need not be polynomial in \(m\) and \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are at most binomially many bases, so any basis-nonrepeating simplex trajectory terminates after at most one fewer pivots.

children.title: Zero-Length Pivots
children.top_down_role: Degenerate exchanges with no corresponding movement of the represented primal point.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis with \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge 0\).
For an entering column \(a_j\), let \(d=B^{-1}a_j\), and assume some \(d_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta=0\) and \(x^{+}=x\), although the basis changes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-simplex definition of a degenerate pivot with no geometric displacement.

source_refs.locator: Part 1. Basic Theory: The Simplex Method and Duality p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pivot step is \[\theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}\frac{(x_B)_i}{d_i}.\] It is a zero-length pivot when \(\theta=0\). Equivalently, at least one eligible leaving row has \((x_B)_i=0\) and attains the ratio-test minimum. The update \(x_B^{+}=x_B-\theta d\), \(x_j^{+}=\theta\) then leaves the represented primal point and its objective value unchanged, while exchanging one basic index for \(j\). Such a pivot can occur only at a degenerate basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-length pivot exchanges basic variables at a degenerate solution while leaving the primal point and objective unchanged.

children.top_down_role: Extended low-progress pivot episodes short of exact basis recurrence.

assumptions_latex: \((B_k,x^k)\) is a sequence of primal-feasible simplex states.
The indices \(k=r,\ldots,s-1\) correspond to consecutive pivots.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stalling sequence is a finite episode \((B_r,x^r),\ldots,(B_s,x^s)\), with \(s>r\), in which every pivot has step length \(\theta_k=0\). Consequently, \(x^{k+1}=x^k\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{k+1}=c^{\mathsf T}x^k\) for every \(k=r,\ldots,s-1\), even though successive bases may differ. Stalling does not itself require a repeated basis; it becomes cycling only if some basis state recurs and the pivot policy reproduces the subsequent exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stalling sequence consists of consecutive zero-length pivots, possibly through distinct bases, with no primal or objective progress.

children.title: Basis Cycling
children.top_down_role: Recurrent basis trajectories under an admissible but nonfinite pivot policy.

assumptions_latex: A fixed linear program is processed in exact arithmetic by a deterministic, memoryless simplex pivot rule with fixed index ordering.
The rule generates admissible basis states \((B_k)_{k\ge 0}\) until it returns an optimality, unboundedness, or infeasibility certificate.
For the fixed problem, each basis uniquely determines the tableau state used by the pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(B_{r+p}=B_r\) for some \(r\ge 0\) and \(p\ge 1\) before termination, then \(B_{r+q+p}=B_{r+q}\) for every \(q\ge 0\), so the rule cycles.

notation.meaning: Length of the recurrent basis cycle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycling under a deterministic memoryless simplex rule is periodic recurrence of an algebraic basis state.

source_refs.locator: Part 1. Basic Theory: The Simplex Method and Duality p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a deterministic, memoryless simplex pivot rule with fixed index ordering, basis cycling occurs when there exist \(r\ge 0\) and \(p\ge 1\) such that \(B_{r+p}=B_r\) before the rule terminates. Because the repeated basis determines the same tableau state, the subsequent choices repeat, giving \(B_{r+q+p}=B_{r+q}\) for every \(q\ge 0\). In primal simplex, a cycle generated by improving admissible pivots consists of degenerate pivots and has constant primal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a deterministic memoryless pivot rule, recurrence of a prior basis reproduces the same subsequent pivots and creates a periodic nonterminating cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Cycling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographic leaving-variable selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic use of hierarchical perturbation coefficients in a degenerate simplex ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the dependence of every basic variable on the hierarchical powers \(\epsilon,\epsilon^2,\ldots,\epsilon^m\) is retained in \(x_B(\epsilon)\). The lexicographic strategy assigns no numerical value to \(\epsilon\). Among the indices admitted by the simplex leaving-variable ratio test, it selects the index \(p\) for which \((x_B(\epsilon))_i/d_i\) is smallest for every sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), implemented by lexicographically comparing the corresponding coefficient sequences. Under the stated hierarchical perturbation this choice is unique. After pivoting, the dependence on every power of \(\epsilon\) is updated for the new basic variables, including the entering variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lexicographic simplex rule keeps epsilon symbolic and compares the coefficient sequences of the eligible ratio-test expressions. It chooses the expression that is smallest for every sufficiently small positive epsilon, yielding a unique leaving index, and propagates all perturbation coefficients through the pivot.
assumptions_latex: x_B(\epsilon)\text{ records the dependence of each basic variable on }\epsilon,\epsilon^2,\ldots,\epsilon^m.
i\text{ ranges over indices admitted by the ordinary leaving-variable ratio test}.
\epsilon>0\text{ is interpreted symbolically and sufficiently small}.
\text{The hierarchical perturbation representation is retained through subsequent pivots}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is the unique eligible index whose ratio }\frac{(x_B(\epsilon))_p}{d_p}\text{ is lexicographically smallest, equivalently smallest for all sufficiently small }\epsilon>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic-solution representation under hierarchical right-hand-side perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial dependence of later simplex basic solutions on a perturbation introduced at an encountered degenerate basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat B\) be the nonsingular basis matrix at an encountered degenerate simplex basis, and set \(v(\epsilon)=(\epsilon,\epsilon^2,\ldots,\epsilon^m)^T\) for \(\epsilon>0\). With \(b(\epsilon)=b+\widehat Bv(\epsilon)\), the basic solution at that basis satisfies \(x_{\widehat{\mathcal B}}(\epsilon)=x_{\widehat{\mathcal B}}+v(\epsilon)\). If the same perturbation is retained and \(B\) is a subsequent nonsingular basis matrix, then \(x_B(\epsilon)=x_B+B^{-1}\widehat Bv(\epsilon)=x_B+\sum_{k=1}^m(B^{-1}\widehat B)_{\cdot k}\epsilon^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbing the right-hand side by the encountered basis matrix times the vector of powers epsilon through epsilon to the m adds those powers directly to the encountered basic solution. At any later nonsingular basis, every basic variable equals its unperturbed value plus a polynomial in epsilon whose coefficient columns come from the change-of-basis matrix.
assumptions_latex: \widehat B\text{ is the nonsingular basis matrix at an encountered degenerate simplex basis}.
\epsilon>0,\quad v(\epsilon)=(\epsilon,\epsilon^2,\ldots,\epsilon^m)^T.
b(\epsilon)=b+\widehat Bv(\epsilon).
B\text{ is a nonsingular basis matrix at a subsequent iteration using the retained perturbation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_B(\epsilon)=x_B+B^{-1}\widehat Bv(\epsilon)=x_B+\sum_{k=1}^m(B^{-1}\widehat B)_{\cdot k}\epsilon^k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate pivots and simplex cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis exchanges with no change in the represented extreme point and closed recurrent sequences of such exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simplex pivot $B\to B'$ is degenerate if the adjacent bases $B$ and $B'$ represent the same extreme-point solution $x^*$. Cycling occurs when a nonempty sequence of degenerate pivots $B_0\to B_1\to\cdots\to B_k$ returns to its initial basis, $B_k=B_0$, with all bases representing the same $x^*$. Consequently, the objective value is constant throughout the cycle. Cycling can occur, so anti-cycling precautions may be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate pivot exchanges adjacent bases without changing the represented extreme point. Cycling is a nonempty closed sequence of such pivots returning to the initial basis; every basis represents the same point, so the objective remains constant. This pathology can occur and may require anti-cycling precautions.
assumptions_latex: $k>0$ and each transition $B_i\to B_{i+1}$ is a simplex pivot.
$B_i$ and $B_{i+1}$ are adjacent bases representing the same extreme point $x^*$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-1$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x(B_i)=x^*\ \forall i,\qquad c^\top x(B_i)=c^\top x^*\ \forall i,\qquad B_k=B_0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate simplex pivots and recurrent-basis cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of strict progress and finite termination when zero-length pivots recur under unchanged deterministic pivot rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a primal-simplex iteration, a pivot is degenerate when the ratio test permits no positive movement of the entering variable. Such a pivot replaces a basis index while leaving the primal point \(x\) and objective value \(c^Tx\) unchanged. If a sequence of degenerate pivots returns to a previously visited basis and the algorithm again applies the same deterministic entering- and leaving-index rules, the same basis sequence is reproduced indefinitely. Thus degeneracy need not cause cycling, but recurrent traversal of a previous basis under unchanged rules causes failure of finite termination unless an anti-cycling safeguard intervenes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate simplex pivot changes the basis without changing the point or objective. Degeneracy alone need not cycle, but if degenerate pivots return to an earlier basis and the same deterministic pivot rules are reused, the basis sequence repeats forever and the algorithm fails to terminate.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a basic feasible primal-simplex iterate with basis }B.
\text{The ratio test gives a zero maximum admissible step for the selected entering variable}.
\text{A subsequent sequence returns to an earlier basis}.
\text{Entering and leaving indices are selected by the same deterministic rules whenever that basis recurs}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^+=x,\quad c^Tx^+=c^Tx\quad\text{for a degenerate pivot, and recurrence of a previous basis under unchanged deterministic rules yields an indefinitely repeating basis cycle}.

children.title: Basis Recurrence versus Vertex Repetition
children.top_down_role: Distinguishes algebraic-state recurrence from repeated geometric representation.

assumptions_latex: Each simplex basis \(B_k\) determines a represented basic feasible point \(x^k\).
Distinct feasible bases are allowed to represent the same degenerate point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(B_r=B_s\), then the associated basic solution is uniquely computed from that basis, so \(x^r=x^s\). The converse fails at a vertex with basis multiplicity: distinct bases \(B_r\ne B_s\) can satisfy \(x^r=x^s\). Therefore repeated visitation of a geometric vertex is not by itself a certificate of basis cycling. A cycling diagnostic must record basis indices, or an equivalent complete tableau state, and detect recurrence of that algebraic state rather than merely equality of primal iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repeated basis forces a repeated vertex, but a degenerate vertex can repeat under distinct bases without basis cycling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographic Positivity Invariance and Finite Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination theorem for lexicographic simplex pivoting from a lexicographically positive initial tableau.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographic Ratio Rule for Degenerate Simplex Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive basis-inverse-column comparisons for resolving a tied feasible-simplex ratio test, including the stated uniqueness and finite-termination consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the minimum-ratio test for entering index \(s\) ties on eligible rows. For each tied row \(r\), compare \(\beta_{r,1}/\widetilde a_{rs}\), where \(\beta_{r,k}\) denotes the row-\(r\), column-\(k\) entry of the current basis inverse. Retain the minimizing rows; if a tie remains, repeat successively with \(\beta_{r,k}/\widetilde a_{rs}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,m\). A unique leaving row is obtained no later than column \(m\). When this rule is used for tied feasible-simplex pivots, the simplex algorithm terminates after finitely many pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When eligible rows tie in the simplex minimum-ratio test, divide their entries from the first basis-inverse column by their respective entering-column coefficients and retain the minimizers. Repeat with successive inverse columns until one row remains. This occurs by the last column, and feasible simplex using this tie-breaking rule terminates finitely.

\text{The minimum-ratio test for entering index }s\text{ has at least two tied eligible rows.}
\widetilde a_{rs}>0\quad\text{for every tied eligible row }r.
\text{The underlying iterations are feasible simplex pivots using this rule whenever a leaving-row tie occurs.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(S\\) be the finite set of admissible pivot states and let \\(L\\) be a totally ordered label set. An ordered-label pivot rule is finite whenever there exists a map \\(\Phi:S\to L^k\\), ordered lexicographically, such that every permitted pivot \\(s\to s'\\) satisfies \\(\Phi(s')<_{\mathrm{lex}}\Phi(s)\\). Under this condition no state can recur, because recurrence would imply a strict lexicographic decrease from \\(\Phi(s)\\) back to itself. Consequently every generated pivot path contains at most \\(|S|-1\\) pivots before reaching a state with no permitted outgoing pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed ordered-label rule terminates if every pivot strictly decreases a lexicographic label on the finite state set.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Based Finite Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sign-vector descent criterion for finite pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(S\\) be a finite pivot-state set, and assign each state a sign vector \\(\sigma(s)\in\{-,0,+\}^q\\). Fix a total order \\(\prec\\) on these sign vectors. A sign-based pivot rule is finite if every selected pivot \\(s\to s'\\) satisfies \\(\sigma(s')\prec\sigma(s)\\), or, when the sign vectors agree, strictly decreases a secondary finite ranking \\(\rho(s)\\). Thus the combined rank \\(\bigl(\sigma(s),\rho(s)\bigr)\\) strictly decreases lexicographically at every pivot, so no state recurs and every maximal pivot path terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign-based rule is finite when its sign vector, supplemented by a finite tie-break rank, strictly decreases at every pivot.

The sign order and secondary ranking remain fixed.
Every selected pivot strictly decreases the combined rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule generates no directed cycle and terminates after at most \\(|S|-1\\) pivots.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Based Finite Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic-orientation criterion for finite pivot paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(G=(V,E)\\) be the finite undirected graph of admissible pivot states and exchanges. An orientation-based pivot rule chooses only arcs of an orientation \\(\vec G\\). The rule is finite if \\(\vec G\\) is acyclic. Equivalently, there exists a topological ranking \\(r:V\to\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\\) such that every allowed pivot \\(u\to v\\) satisfies \\(r(u)<r(v)\\). Every rule-generated path then visits each state at most once and contains at most \\(|V|-1\\) pivots before reaching a sink of \\(\vec G\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directing the finite pivot graph acyclically makes every orientation-respecting pivot path finite and bounds it by the number of states minus one.
assumptions_latex: \\(G\\) is finite.
The orientation is fixed during the run.
The pivot rule follows only oriented arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acyclicity of \\(\vec G\\) implies termination within \\(|V|-1\\) pivots.

standard_field_rationale: a finite directed graph is acyclic exactly when it admits a topological ordering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of primal-feasible basis pivoting under an anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-state termination theorem for complementary pivot systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(S\\) be the finite set of admissible complementary bases, where each complementary pair contributes at most one basic label. The interpretation of that terminal basis as a solution or certificate depends on the underlying complementarity problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-to-Vertex Quotient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient of feasible bases by equality of represented basic solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible basis \(B\), define \(q(B)=x^B\) by \(x_B^B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(x_N^B=0\). Define \(B\sim B'\) exactly when \(q(B)=q(B')\). The induced map \(\bar q\) is a bijection between equivalence classes of feasible bases and vertices represented by feasible bases. For a standard-form polyhedron, every vertex is represented by a feasible basis, so \(\bar q\) is a bijection onto \(V_P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathcal B\to V_P\) map each feasible basis to its basic feasible solution. The fiber over a vertex \(v\) is \(q^{-1}(v)=\{B\in\mathcal B:x^B=v\}\). Quotienting can therefore collapse multiple basis edges and degenerate pivot steps. knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Rule Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional-graph representation of a deterministic memoryless improving pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite polyhedral graph whose edges are oriented by a generic objective toward improvement, with unique sink \(v^*\). A deterministic memoryless pivot rule is a map \(\rho:V\setminus\{v^*\}\to V\) such that \((v,\rho(v))\) is an outgoing oriented edge. The selected arcs \(v\to\rho(v)\) form an in-arborescence rooted at \(v^*\): every nonroot vertex has one selected outgoing arc, the root has none, and repeated application of \(\rho\) reaches \(v^*\). The rule-induced path from \(v\) is \(v,\rho(v),\rho^2(v),\ldots,v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic memoryless improving rule selects one outgoing edge per nonoptimal vertex; strict improvement makes these choices an arborescence directed toward the optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Vertex Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic two-objective shadow-vertex trajectory on a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an auxiliary objective \(d\), a target objective \(c\), and a known \(d\)-maximizing vertex. Starting at the projected \(d\)-maximizer, traverse the appropriate boundary chain of the polygon \(\pi(P)\) toward its \(c\)-maximizing point, lifting each projected edge to the corresponding adjacent vertices of \(P\). knowledge_statements.title: Parametric-Objective Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective continuation through adjacent normal cones of a fixed feasible polyhedron.

Continue until \(\lambda=1\). With nondegenerate breakpoints and bounded optima throughout, the resulting finite basis sequence traces adjacent normal cones and ends at a basis optimal for \(c^1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Graph Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unoriented edge distance in the one-skeleton of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(P)=(V,E)\) be the undirected vertex-edge graph of a polyhedron \(P\). knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Path Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest directed distance under a fixed linear-objective orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and orient every edge \(uv\) from \(u\) to \(v\) whenever \(c^\top u<c^\top v\). knowledge_statements.title: Least-Usage Tie Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible deterministic or randomized completion of least-usage pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_t\) be the eligible entering indices and let \(h_j(t)\) be their usage counters. The least-usage tie set is \[T_t=\{j\in E_t:h_j(t)=\min_{k\in E_t}h_k(t)\}.\] A tie regime is admissible for the least-usage family precisely when it selects \(e_t\in T_t\) whenever \(T_t\neq\varnothing\). Examples include choosing the smallest index in \(T_t\), applying a fixed cyclic priority restricted to \(T_t\), or sampling from a distribution supported on \(T_t\). Different admissible regimes may generate different pivot paths and iteration counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cunningham Recency Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-recently-considered pricing implemented by a persistent cyclic scan pointer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cyclic order of all variable indices and retain the index most recently selected for entry. At the next primal-simplex iteration, scan the cyclic order beginning immediately after that index and choose the first nonbasic index \(j\) satisfying \(\bar c_j<0\). Perform the ratio test and pivot, then set the retained index to \(j\). If a complete scan finds no eligible index, stop and declare the current basic feasible solution optimal. An initial retained position and deterministic rules for degeneracy and leaving-variable ties complete the specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resume a cyclic scan after the last entering variable and choose the first currently improving nonbasic variable encountered.
assumptions_latex: A fixed cyclic order and initial scan position are given.
The current basis is primal feasible.
Degenerate and leaving-variable ties have prescribed resolutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: j^*=\text{first }j\text{ after the retained position with }\bar c_j<0

children.title: Round-Robin Pivot Rules

knowledge_statements.title: Round-Robin Pivot Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed cyclic-priority pricing with a persistent scan position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cyclic ordering \((i_1,\ldots,i_n)\) and a pointer \(p_t\). At iteration \(t\), inspect indices \(i_{p_t},i_{p_t+1},\ldots\) cyclically until encountering the first eligible nonbasic variable \(i_q\) with negative reduced cost. Choose \(i_q\) to enter, perform the ratio test and pivot, and set \(p_{t+1}=q+1\) modulo \(n\). If one full cycle contains no eligible variable, stop with the current basic feasible solution. A deterministic leaving-variable and degeneracy convention is required to make the entire basis sequence unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan variables cyclically from a saved pointer, pivot on the first improving candidate, and resume at the following position.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is primal feasible.
A cyclic order and initial pointer are fixed.
Leaving-variable and degeneracy ties have fixed resolutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{t+1}=q+1\pmod n

first eligible index found by the scan

children.title: Cyclic Order Memory Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Order Memory Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite-memory cyclic pricing regimes for simplex entering-variable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set containing all variable labels, let \(\pi\) be a cyclic ordering of \(V\), and let \(p_k\in V\) be the stored pointer at iteration \(k\). For the current nonbasic-label set \(N_k\subseteq V\), let \(E_k\subseteq N_k\) contain exactly the labels eligible to enter with strict objective improvement. If \(E_k\ne\varnothing\), the rule selects the first member \(e_k\) of \(E_k\) encountered while scanning \(\pi\) from \(p_k\). After a pivot with leaving label \(\ell_k\), it updates the pointer by a prescribed map \(U:V\times V\times V\to V\), so that \(p_{k+1}=U(p_k,e_k,\ell_k)\). If the current basis is feasible and \(E_k=\varnothing\), the reduced-cost optimality condition holds and the rule declares the basis optimal. Different choices of \(U\) specify different cyclic-order memory regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclic-order memory rule scans a fixed cyclic order of all variable labels from a persistent pointer, selects the first improving nonbasic candidate, and updates the pointer after each pivot. At a feasible basis, it declares optimality only when no improving nonbasic candidate exists.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and cyclically ordered by \(\pi\).
The current simplex basis is feasible.
\(E_k\) contains all and only currently nonbasic labels satisfying the strict-improvement eligibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(E_k\ne\varnothing\), then \(e_k=\operatorname{first}_{\pi,p_k}(E_k)\) and \(p_{k+1}=U(p_k,e_k,\ell_k)\); if \(E_k=\varnothing\), the current feasible basis satisfies the reduced-cost optimality condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Edge Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical random-edge rule on the improving graph of a bounded linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded polytope \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), objective \(c\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and current vertex \(v_k\), let \(I(v_k)=\{w: [v_k,w]\text{ is an edge of }P,\ c^\top w<c^\top v_k\}\). If \(I(v_k)=\varnothing\), stop and output \(v_k\). Otherwise sample \(v_{k+1}\) uniformly from \(I(v_k)\) and repeat. Thus, conditional on the current vertex, every improving adjacent vertex has probability \(1/|I(v_k)|\) of being selected. For a nondegenerate simplex tableau, this is equivalently uniform selection among improving feasible pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-edge repeatedly chooses uniformly among improving adjacent vertices and stops when none exists.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded polytope with a finite vertex-edge graph.
The objective is minimized.
For the tableau interpretation, the linear program is nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(v_{k+1}=w\mid v_k)=|I(v_k)|^{-1}\) for every \(w\in I(v_k)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Facet Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive random-facet scheme for a bounded nondegenerate polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bounded nondegenerate polytope \(P\), objective \(c\), and feasible vertex \(v\), choose uniformly a facet \(F\) of \(P\) not containing \(v\). Recursively optimize \(c\) over \(F\), starting from a vertex of \(F\) reachable by the rule's prescribed facet-entry pivot sequence, and obtain \(x_F\). If no edge incident to \(x_F\) leaves \(F\) with strict objective decrease, output \(x_F\); otherwise take such a decreasing edge to a vertex outside \(F\) and recursively continue on \(P\). The base case is a zero-dimensional face, whose unique vertex is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-facet recursively optimizes on a uniformly selected facet, then either certifies optimality or leaves that facet along an improving edge.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded and nondegenerate.
Every recursive facet subproblem is supplied a feasible starting vertex.
The objective is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion returns a vertex with no incident edge of strict objective decrease.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Variable Priorities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-priority resolution of simultaneously eligible simplex variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be the finite set of variable labels. If \(E_k=\varnothing\), stop; otherwise choose the unique \(e_k\in E_k\) having smallest rank under \(\Pi\), perform the associated ratio test and pivot, and retain the same permutation for subsequent iterations. A resampled-priority variant instead draws an independent permutation \(\Pi_k\) before each selection; the sampling schedule is part of the rule specification.

The eligible set is determined before random priority resolves the choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{j\in E_k}\operatorname{rank}_{\Pi}(j)\), or the analogous expression with \(\Pi_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected pivot bound for a randomized Bland ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A randomized simplex pivot rule fixes a uniformly random ordering of the variables, uses that ordering for Bland's entering-variable selection, and selects the leaving variable lexicographically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a variable-index permutation uniformly at random before simplex pivoting begins. Use Bland's rule relative to this fixed ordering to select the entering variable, and use the lexicographic method to select the leaving variable. There is a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every linear program with at most \(n\) variables and at most \(n\) constraints, \[\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{pivot}}]\leq \exp\!\left(C\sqrt{n\ln n}\right),\] where the expectation is over the initial permutation. The displayed upper bound is subexponential in \(n\), but it is not a polynomial bound.

For every linear program with at most n variables and at most n constraints, the expected number of pivots is at most exp(C sqrt(n log n)) for some positive constant C, with expectation over the initial ordering. This upper bound is subexponential but not polynomial.

\text{A variable-index permutation is sampled uniformly before pivoting and then held fixed.}

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Tie Breakers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomization confined to ties under a deterministic primary pivot score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(E_k\) be the finite eligible pivot set and let \(s_k:E_k\to\mathbb{R}\) be a deterministic primary score, with smaller values preferred. If \(E_k=\varnothing\), stop under the underlying simplex stopping convention. Otherwise define \(T_k=\{p\in E_k:s_k(p)=\min_{q\in E_k}s_k(q)\}\), sample the selected pivot \(p_k\) uniformly from \(T_k\), execute it, and continue. Randomness therefore changes only the resolution of equal primary scores and never selects a pivot whose primary score is worse than the deterministic optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the deterministic pivot score first, then choose the selected pivot uniformly among exactly tied best pivots.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) is finite.
The primary score \(s_k\) is fixed before tie-breaking randomness is drawn.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For nonempty \(E_k\), \(\Pr(p_k=p\mid E_k,s_k)=|T_k|^{-1}\) for every \(p\in T_k\), and \(\Pr(p_k=p\mid E_k,s_k)=0\) for every \(p\in E_k\setminus T_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Priority–Tie Randomization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates persistent priority randomness from local tie-breaking randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_k\) be the eligible pivot set. A priority–tie randomization regime is represented by a random priority state \(R_k\), a deterministic score \(s_k(p;R_k)\), and a conditional distribution \(\mu_k\) supported on \(T_k(R_k)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{p\in E_k}s_k(p;R_k)\). The selected pivot satisfies \(p_k\sim\mu_k(\cdot\mid T_k(R_k))\). Priority randomization occurs when \(R_k\) changes the ordering of unequal candidates; tie randomization occurs when \(R_k\) leaves the primary scores fixed and \(\mu_k\) alone resolves multiplicity. The regime must specify whether \(R_k\) is persistent, periodically refreshed, or independently resampled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime consists of a random priority state, a score-induced best set, a distribution on that set, and a stated resampling schedule.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) is finite and nonempty when selection occurs.
\(\mu_k\) assigns probability one to the score-minimizing set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(p_k\in T_k(R_k)\mid E_k,R_k)=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Pricing Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex pricing restricted to managed subsets of nonbasic variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition or cover the nonbasic-variable labels by managed sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\). If an improving member is found, select one by the prescribed within-set rule and pivot. If none is found, advance the active-set index and price another managed set. Declare optimality only after every currently nonbasic variable has been priced without finding an improving reduced cost since the most recent basis change. After a pivot, update or restart the active-set schedule as specified by the implementation.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Candidate Pricing

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Pivot Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouped basis exchange in a simplex-type method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a basis \(B_k\) of rank \(m\), choose entering and leaving blocks \(E_k\) and \(L_k\) with \(|E_k|=|L_k|\ge 1\), \(E_k\cap B_k=\varnothing\), and \(L_k\subseteq B_k\). Form \(B_{k+1}=(B_k\setminus L_k)\cup E_k\) only if the corresponding basis matrix is nonsingular and the resulting basic solution is feasible. Accept the block exchange when it satisfies the rule's stated descent or lexicographic-improvement test. If no admissible improving block exists, the method must perform a complete reduced-cost optimality test before stopping; otherwise it updates the factorization and repeats.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-pivot rule exchanges equally sized entering and leaving sets while preserving basis rank and feasibility, and accepts only a specified improvement.
assumptions_latex: The current basis matrix is nonsingular and its basic solution is feasible.
Block admissibility includes nonsingularity and feasibility of the proposed basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{k+1}=(B_k\setminus L_k)\cup E_k\) is a feasible basis of rank \(m\) whenever the block pivot is accepted.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Parameterized Pivot Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case simplex pivot count viewed as a function of dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a pivot rule \(R\) and an admissible class \(\mathcal{L}_{d}\) of linear programs whose feasible polyhedra have dimension \(d\). The dimension-parameterized worst-case pivot count is \[P_R^{\mathrm{dim}}(d)=\sup_{L\in\mathcal{L}_{d}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_0(L)}T_R(L,B).\] Any restriction on constraints, encoding length, degeneracy, or randomness must be stated separately; without such restrictions this quantity need not be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This measure takes the worst pivot count over admissible dimension-d instances and starting bases, with nontermination counted as infinity.
assumptions_latex: The pivot rule \(R\), admissible instance class, and allowed starting bases are fixed.
Pivot count, rather than arithmetic work, is the resource measured.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_R^{\mathrm{dim}}(d)\) is the supremal pivot count at structural dimension \(d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Bit Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Time–Space Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of attainable runtime-memory pairs for equivalent simplex implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal I\), computational platform \(P\), correctness criterion, and a family \(\mathcal S\) of simplex implementations. knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Sensitive Pivot Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of deterministic simplex pivot decisions on positive row rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b\}\). For a positive diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), the representation \(DAx\le Db\) defines the same feasible polyhedron. Let \(\Phi(s;A,b,c)\) denote the complete decision of a deterministic simplex rule at state \(s\), including entering and leaving choices and deterministic tie-breaking. The rule is invariant under positive row scaling if corresponding reachable states satisfy \(\Phi(s;A,b,c)=\Phi(s;DA,Db,c)\). If, after a common decision history, corresponding reachable states yield different decisions, the next bases differ, so the two equivalent representations can generate different subsequent basis paths and pivot counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row scaling preserves the feasible linear program, but a deterministic simplex rule can follow a different basis path when its complete pivot decision is not invariant at a corresponding reachable state.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\) with \(d_i>0\) for every \(i\)
The pivot rule and all tie-breaking conventions are deterministic
Bases and simplex states are compared under the natural correspondence between the two row-scaled representations
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If corresponding reachable states satisfy \(\Phi(s;A,b,c)\ne\Phi(s;DA,Db,c)\), the basis paths diverge at that decision and may have different pivot counts.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial, exponential, worst-case, and average-case complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the regimes and illustrates their distinction using simplex, ellipsoid, and interior-point methods; average-case claims require a specified input distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let T_A(x) be the running time of algorithm A on an instance x of size n=|x|. The algorithm is polynomial if there exists a polynomial p such that \(\forall x,\ T_A(x)\le p(|x|)\); an exponential algorithm may require time growing exponentially with n. Worst-case analysis bounds \(\sup_{|x|=n}T_A(x)\), whereas average-case analysis studies \(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(x)]\) for a specified distribution \(D_n\). For linear programming, these regimes can differ sharply: simplex has exponential worst-case behavior but polynomial average behavior under the distributions considered, while ellipsoid and most interior-point methods have polynomial worst-case guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial algorithm is guaranteed to solve every instance in time polynomial in its size, whereas an exponential algorithm may require exponentially growing time. Worst-case analysis bounds every instance of a given size; average-case analysis takes expected running time under an explicitly chosen input distribution. In linear programming, simplex illustrates a large gap between exponential worst-case and polynomial average behavior under the distributions considered, while the ellipsoid method and most interior-point methods have polynomial worst-case guarantees.
assumptions_latex: A is an algorithm on instances x with size measure \(n=|x|\).
Average-case performance is evaluated relative to a specified family of input distributions \(D_n\).
The LP method classifications concern the algorithmic variants and distributional models under discussion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{polynomiality is a uniform per-instance guarantee, while average-case complexity is distribution-dependent and need not match worst-case complexity.}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A combinatorial pivot bound when polytope dimension is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a simple \(d\)-dimensional polytope described by \(m\) facet inequalities, and let the objective be generic on its vertices. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-ratio leaving-variable rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies after choosing an entering variable in a primal-feasible simplex dictionary. The stated rule requires at least one positive pivot-column coefficient; ties permit multiple leaving choices.

children.title: Polynomial Diameter Problem

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Diameter Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The open polynomial upper-bound predicate for general polyhedral diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial diameter property asks whether there exists a fixed bivariate polynomial \(p\) such that every \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron \(P\) described by \(m\) facets satisfies \[\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le p(d,m).\] Equivalently, with \(\Delta(d,m)\) denoting the maximum such diameter, the question is whether \(\Delta(d,m)\) is polynomially bounded jointly in \(d\) and \(m\). No general polynomial bound or superpolynomial lower bound is presently known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: It remains open whether every polyhedral graph has diameter bounded by one polynomial in its dimension and number of facets.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron described by \(m\) facets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unresolved predicate is \(\exists p\in\mathbb R[d,m]\ \forall P:\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le p(d,m)\).
review_flags: The current open-status claim requires a contemporary authoritative source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition accurately formulates the polynomial-diameter question, but the assertion that neither a polynomial upper bound nor a superpolynomial lower bound is currently known is time-sensitive and needs a contemporary authoritative source.

children.title: Monotone Hirsch Family

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Hirsch Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hirsch-type bounds for paths directed by a generic linear objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(d\)-polytope with \(m\) facets and let \(c\) take distinct values on adjacent vertices. Orient every edge from lower to higher \(c\)-value. The monotone Hirsch assertion requires every vertex to admit a directed path to the unique maximizing vertex using at most \(m-d\) edges. This assertion is stronger than the corresponding undirected diameter bound and is false in general; consequently, short undirected paths do not ensure Hirsch-length objective-monotone simplex paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The monotone Hirsch assertion bounds every improving path-to-optimum distance by facets minus dimension, but this stronger assertion fails generally.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded \(d\)-polytope with \(m\) facets.
The linear objective \(c\) is generic on edges and has a unique maximizing vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The universal monotone bound \(\operatorname{dist}^{+}_c(v,v_c^*)\le m-d\) is false.
review_flags: A precise counterexample source and the intended monotone-Hirsch convention are required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is suitable, but monotone Hirsch formulations differ over starting vertices and endpoint requirements. A precise source is needed to establish the intended convention and its counterexample.

children.title: Short-Path versus Local-Rule Gap
children.top_down_role: The boundary between existence of a short monotone path and its discovery by a uniform local policy.

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Path versus Local-Rule Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary between path existence and uniform local discovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance class \(\mathcal I\), the existence statement \[\forall I\in\mathcal I\ \exists\text{ an improving path }p_I:\ |p_I|\le q(|I|)\] does not imply the algorithmic statement \[\exists\text{ a uniform local pivot rule }R\ \forall I\in\mathcal I:\ |R(I)|\le q'(|I|).\] The first statement may select a different globally informed path for every instance; the second requires one rule whose decision uses only its prescribed local state. Therefore a polynomial monotone diameter bound alone is not a polynomial pivot-rule guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short improving path may exist for every instance without any single locally informed pivot rule finding short paths on all instances.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) chooses pivots using only a prescribed local state.
\(q\) and \(q'\) are polynomial bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall I\,\exists p_I)\) does not by itself entail \((\exists R\,\forall I)\).

children.title: Oriented-Matroid Programming Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Oriented-Matroid Programming Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial encoding of feasibility, adjacency, and objective improvement by signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oriented-matroid program consists of an oriented matroid \(\mathcal M\) on a finite ground set together with distinguished elements \(g\) and \(f\), representing homogenization and objective directions. Feasible states are encoded by covectors satisfying the designated constraint signs and positive \(g\)-sign; adjacent states differ by an admissible basis exchange. The signed circuits and cocircuits determine whether such an exchange improves the \(f\)-direction. When \(\mathcal M\) is realizable by a real vector configuration, these states and exchanges recover the corresponding linear-programming bases and simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oriented-matroid programming represents feasible bases, adjacent exchanges, and objective improvement using only circuit and cocircuit signs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is an oriented matroid with distinguished nonloop elements \(g\) and \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible pivot paths are representable through covector signs and admissible basis exchanges of \(\mathcal M\).

children.title: Acyclic Unique-Sink Orientation Interface
children.top_down_role: The local-improvement abstraction for oriented cube-like graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Unique-Sink Orientation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic unique-sink orientations as abstract local-improvement systems on cubes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An acyclic unique-sink orientation of the \(n\)-cube is an orientation of its graph that is acyclic and whose restriction to every nonempty face has exactly one sink. In particular, the whole cube has a unique global sink. A local improvement algorithm starts at a vertex and repeatedly selects an outgoing incident edge; acyclicity guarantees termination, and the unique-sink property makes the terminal vertex the global sink. The number of traversed edges is the abstract pivot complexity of the chosen local rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclic cube orientation with one sink on every face models local improvement; following outgoing edges terminates at the unique global sink.
assumptions_latex: The underlying graph is the graph of the \(n\)-dimensional cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every walk that repeatedly follows an outgoing edge terminates at the unique global sink.
review_flags: A standard source for the AUSO definition and pivot interpretation is required.

children.title: Realizability Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Realizability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer limits between abstract unique-sink orientations and geometric linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\) be the orientations induced by generic linear objectives on realizations of combinatorial \(n\)-cubes, and let \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{AUSO}}(n)\) be all acyclic unique-sink orientations of the abstract \(n\)-cube. Then \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\subseteq\mathcal O_{\mathrm{AUSO}}(n)\), while abstract orientations need not be realizable by linear programs. Consequently, an upper bound proved for every AUSO transfers to realizable cube linear programs, but a lower-bound AUSO instance transfers only after its realizability is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LP-induced cube orientations are AUSOs, but abstract AUSO lower bounds apply to simplex paths only when the orientation is geometrically realizable.
assumptions_latex: Objectives inducing orientations are generic on every edge.
Realizations have the combinatorial face lattice of an \(n\)-cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal AUSO upper bounds transfer to \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{LP}}(n)\), whereas individual lower bounds require realizability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pivot Count as a Surrogate for Simplex Solve Effort
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A measurement convention for simplex solve effort, with the boundary on comparisons across algorithm classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an iterative method, execution time is determined by both the number of iterations and the work per iteration. The iteration count is a machine-independent surrogate for execution time when the algorithms being compared have approximately comparable per-iteration costs. It is not a meaningful time surrogate across substantially different algorithm classes whose per-iteration costs differ. For linear programming by the simplex method, this effort measure is the number of pivots required to solve the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative algorithm's running time depends on both its iteration count and its cost per iteration. Iteration count is a machine-independent proxy for running time when the compared algorithms have roughly comparable per-iteration costs, but it is not meaningful for time comparisons across substantially different algorithm classes. For the simplex method, the chosen iteration measure is the number of pivots needed to solve the linear program.
assumptions_latex: \text{The algorithms under comparison are iterative.}

children.title: Benchmark-Composition Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of reported behavior on benchmark selection and aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark-Composition Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes how benchmark mixture and aggregation determine a reported simplex-performance statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let benchmark strata be indexed by \(k=1,\ldots,K\), with stratum weight \(w_k\ge 0\), \(\sum_k w_k=1\), and within-stratum mean performance \(\mu_k\). The benchmark-wide arithmetic mean is \(M(w)=\sum_k w_k\mu_k\). Hence two benchmark compositions \(w\) and \(v\) report a difference \[M(w)-M(v)=\sum_{k=1}^K (w_k-v_k)\mu_k.\] Unless all \(\mu_k\) are equal, the reported mean can change solely because the stratum weights change, even when every within-stratum result remains fixed. Medians, shifted geometric means, and timeout conventions define different aggregation functionals and need not preserve solver rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate simplex performance depends on the benchmark mixture and summary statistic; changing either can alter reported results or solver rankings without changing any individual run.
assumptions_latex: \(K<\infty\) and every reported observation has a fixed stratum assignment.
\(w,v\) are probability vectors over the same strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(w)-M(v)=\sum_k(w_k-v_k)\mu_k\), so composition invariance holds for all \(w,v\) only if \(\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_K\).

notation.meaning: proportion of benchmark instances assigned to stratum k

children.title: Pivot Count versus Runtime Evidence
children.top_down_role: The empirical distinction between short paths and inexpensive solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Count versus Runtime Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the combinatorial path length from the computational work incurred along that path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a completed simplex run with \(N\) accepted pivots, write its runtime as \[T=T_0+\sum_{t=1}^{N}\bigl(P_t+B_t+O_t\bigr),\] where \(P_t\) is pricing work, \(B_t\) is basis-solve, update, and refactorization work, and \(O_t\) is remaining per-iteration overhead. Pivot count alone determines runtime only under a model that controls these terms uniformly. Consequently, \(N_A<N_B\) does not imply \(T_A<T_B\): run \(A\) may perform fewer but more expensive pivots. Empirical claims about short pivot paths and inexpensive solves must therefore report these as distinct response variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smaller pivot count need not mean a shorter runtime because pricing, basis updates, refactorizations, and other costs vary among pivots and runs.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is measured for the same stopping convention across compared runs.
\(P_t,B_t,O_t\ge 0\) represent disjoint accounted work categories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_A<N_B\not\Rightarrow T_A<T_B\) without additional bounds on per-pivot work.
review_flags: The cost decomposition is standard, but a source on empirical simplex pivot-count/runtime comparisons is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between pivot count and runtime matches the terminal container, and the accounting identity is coherent when its work terms are defined as measured time contributions. No citation supports the empirical guidance or this particular decomposition.

children.title: Candidate-Selection Cost
children.top_down_role: Pricing effort attached to locating and ranking entering candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Selection Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts pricing work required to identify an eligible entering variable in revised primal simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(t\) of revised primal simplex, let \(q_t\) nonbasic columns be inspected and let computing or updating one reduced cost require at most \(C_{r,t}\) arithmetic operations. If ranking the inspected candidates costs \(C_{s,t}(q_t)\), then candidate-selection work satisfies \[P_t\le q_tC_{r,t}+C_{s,t}(q_t).\] Full pricing has \(q_t=n-m\); partial pricing may use \(q_t<n-m\), but must retain a rule for eventually inspecting every persistently eligible candidate. With a dense basis solve used separately to obtain the pricing multiplier, a column reduced cost requires \(O(m)\) arithmetic operations, giving \(P_t=O(mq_t+C_{s,t}(q_t))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing cost is bounded by the number of inspected nonbasic columns times the cost per reduced cost, plus the cost of ranking candidates.
assumptions_latex: The basis matrix is nonsingular and the pricing multiplier is available.
Arithmetic-operation count is the resource measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_t\le q_tC_{r,t}+C_{s,t}(q_t)\), and dense column pricing gives \(P_t=O(mq_t+C_{s,t}(q_t))\).

notation.meaning: number of nonbasic candidates inspected at iteration t
operation bound for one reduced-cost evaluation

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses total work as the joint effect of pricing effort and the pivot trajectory it induces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a pricing policy \(\pi\) generate \(N_\pi\) accepted pivots. If \(P_t^\pi\) is candidate-selection work and \(B_t^\pi\) is basis-processing work at pivot \(t\), define total modeled work by \[W(\pi)=\sum_{t=1}^{N_\pi}\bigl(P_t^\pi+B_t^\pi\bigr).\] A policy with stronger candidate evaluation can have \(P_t^\pi>P_t^\rho\) while producing a smaller \(N_\pi\) or cheaper later bases. Thus neither minimum per-iteration pricing cost nor minimum pivot count alone minimizes \(W\). Comparing pricing policies requires evaluating the complete induced trajectory under a common implementation and stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More expensive pricing may produce a shorter or cheaper pivot path; total work, rather than pricing cost or pivot count alone, captures the tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: Each policy starts from the same initial basis and uses the same feasibility and stopping tolerances.
All work terms use one common resource measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Policy quality is ordered by \(W(\pi)\), which is not determined by \(P_t^\pi\) or \(N_\pi\) alone.

notation.meaning: pivot count induced by policy pi
total modeled pricing and basis-processing work

children.title: Basis-Processing Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Processing Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposes accepted-pivot work into basis solves, factor updates, and periodic refactorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_t\) be the basis matrix before pivot \(t\). Suppose the implementation performs \(s_t\) triangular solves using stored factors, a factor update after the pivot, and a full refactorization when \(t\) belongs to a set \(R\). If their operation counts are \(C_{\mathrm{solve},t}\), \(C_{\mathrm{upd},t}\), and \(C_{\mathrm{ref},t}\), then basis-processing work through \(N\) pivots is \[W_B=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(s_tC_{\mathrm{solve},t}+C_{\mathrm{upd},t}+\mathbf 1_{\{t\in R\}}C_{\mathrm{ref},t}\right).\] For dense matrices, conventional bounds are \(C_{\mathrm{solve},t}=O(m^2)\) and \(C_{\mathrm{ref},t}=O(m^3)\); sparse costs depend on fill and factor structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis-processing work is the sum of factor solves, pivot updates, and occasional refactorizations; dense and sparse implementations can have very different costs.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted pivot preserves a nonsingular \(m\times m\) basis.
Arithmetic operations are counted, excluding pricing and external overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_B=\sum_t(s_tC_{\mathrm{solve},t}+C_{\mathrm{upd},t}+\mathbf 1_{\{t\in R\}}C_{\mathrm{ref},t})\).

children.title: Numerical Perturbation Strategies
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision perturbation families used to separate degenerate choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Perturbation Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies bounded finite perturbations intended to separate degenerate ratio-test choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), objective \(c^Tx\), and scales \(s_i>0\), choose signs or distinct ranks \(r_i\) and a magnitude \(\varepsilon>0\). Form perturbed data \(b_i'=b_i+\varepsilon r_is_i\) or, for objective tie separation, \(c_j'=c_j+\varepsilon r_js_j\). Run simplex on the perturbed problem using fixed feasibility and optimality tolerances. Reduce \(\varepsilon\) and restart or recover the original problem whenever the perturbation exceeds its prescribed relative bound or changes original-problem feasibility beyond tolerance. Output a basis only after checking it against unperturbed \(A,b,c\). Finite perturbation encourages separated comparisons but does not itself prove absence of cycling under roundoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small ranked perturbations separate degenerate choices, but their magnitude must be controlled and the resulting basis must be checked against the original linear program.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The perturbation scales and admissible relative bound are specified before the run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns only a basis satisfying the unperturbed feasibility and optimality checks within the declared tolerances.

children.title: Pivot Eligibility Tolerances

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Eligibility Tolerances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tolerance-based entering and leaving eligibility for a primal revised-simplex iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), let \(B\) be a primal-feasible basis, \(y=B^{-T}c_B\), and \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^Ty\) for each nonbasic \(j\). Given dual tolerance \(\tau_d\ge0\), column \(j\) is entering-eligible only if \(\bar c_j< -\tau_d\). With direction \(d=B^{-1}a_j\), row \(i\) is leaving-eligible only if \(d_i>\tau_p\), where \(\tau_p\ge0\) is the pivot tolerance. If no entering column is eligible, the basis is declared optimal only to tolerance; if an entering column has no leaving-eligible row, unboundedness requires an additional direction-validity check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entering variable must improve beyond the dual tolerance, and a leaving row must have a sufficiently positive pivot coefficient; terminal declarations remain tolerance-dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and its basic solution satisfies the declared primal feasibility tolerance.
The linear program is in minimization standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eligibility is given by \(\bar c_j< -\tau_d\) and \(d_i>\tau_p\).

notation.meaning: reduced cost of nonbasic column j

review_flags: Needs a numerical simplex reference for the exact tolerance conventions and terminal safeguards.

children.title: Ratio-Test Tie Management

knowledge_statements.title: Ratio-Test Tie Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a deterministic tolerance-aware rule for resolving near-ties in the primal ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an entering column with direction \(d=B^{-1}a_j\), form eligible ratios \(\theta_i=x_{B_i}/d_i\) over rows satisfying \(d_i>\tau_p\). Let \(\theta_*=
\min_i\theta_i\) and define the tie set \(I=\{i:\theta_i\le\theta_*+\tau_r\max(1,|\theta_*|)\}\). Choose the leaving row from \(I\) by a fixed secondary rule, such as smallest basic-variable index or a lexicographic comparison of normalized tableau rows. Reject a pivot whose computed element fails the stability threshold, and try the next tied row. Stop with failure status if no tied row passes the threshold; otherwise pivot and record the selected rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collect ratios indistinguishable within tolerance, resolve them deterministically, and reject numerically unsafe pivot elements before updating the basis.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B\) is primal feasible within the declared feasibility tolerance.
At least one row satisfies \(d_i>\tau_p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The leaving row is selected deterministically from the tolerance-defined tie set \(I\), subject to the pivot-stability check.

notation.meaning: set of ratio-test rows treated as tied

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Tie Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when finite tolerances merge mathematically distinct ratio-test candidates or split exact ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider two eligible ratio-test values \(\theta_1\le\theta_2\) and a tie threshold \(\delta=\tau_r\max(1,|\theta_1|)\). The rule treating candidates as tied exactly when \(\theta_2-\theta_1\le\delta\) has three regimes: a resolved regime when the computed gap exceeds \(\delta\); a tolerance-tie regime when the computed gap is at most \(\delta\); and an uncertainty regime when the rounding-error bound \(e\) satisfies \(|(\widehat\theta_2-
\widehat\theta_1)-
\delta|\le e\). In the uncertainty regime, admissible roundoff can reverse the tie classification, so the leaving decision is not robust without increased precision or a secondary anti-cycling rule.

assumptions_latex: \(\widehat\theta_i\) are computed ratios with a certified gap-error bound \(e\ge0\).
The same relative tie rule is applied to both candidates.

If \(|(\widehat\theta_2-
\widehat\theta_1)-
\delta|\le e\), tie classification is not guaranteed invariant under admissible roundoff.
