review_flags: Needs a numerical-analysis source for ratio-test error bounds and tolerance-sensitive classification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. However, the uncertainty criterion assumes an error bound for the relevant gap-to-threshold quantity, while the threshold itself depends on a ratio value. A numerical-analysis source and a fully specified propagated-error model are needed.

children.title: Adaptive Anti-Stalling Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing adaptations intended to leave extended low-progress regimes.

assumptions_latex: All objective values use one scaling convention.
The escape rule eventually performs a complete eligible-candidate scan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active pricing rule is \(\pi_1\) after \(L\) consecutive observations with \(g_t\le\eta\), and remains so until \(g_t>\eta\).

notation.meaning: normalized objective progress after pivot t

review_flags: Needs a source for a concrete adaptive anti-stalling pricing rule and its progress criterion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switches pricing behavior after a declared sequence of low-progress simplex iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a progress threshold \(\eta>0\), a window length \(L\ge1\), and a baseline pricing rule \(\pi_0\). After pivot \(t\), compute normalized progress \(g_t=|z_{t+1}-z_t|/\max(1,|z_t|)\). Declare stalling when \(g_s\le\eta\) for each of the last \(L\) accepted pivots. While not stalled, use \(\pi_0\). When stalled, switch for at least one complete candidate scan to a declared escape rule \(\pi_1\), such as expanded pricing, a weighted reduced-cost rule, or deterministic anti-cycling selection. Return to \(\pi_0\) only after progress exceeds \(\eta\); terminate solely by the solver's feasibility, optimality, or limit tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detect a window of negligible objective progress, temporarily strengthen or alter pricing, and return to baseline only after measurable progress resumes.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Anti-Stalling Pricing

children.title: Solver Path Transitions
children.top_down_role: Interfaces where a solver changes pivot framework or obtains a basis from another algorithm.

children.title: Primal–Dual Simplex Switching
children.top_down_role: Transitions between primal-feasible and dual-feasible pivot trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and primal and dual residuals are evaluated consistently.
The problem is a minimization linear program in standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each selected simplex mode begins from the approximate feasibility condition it preserves; when neither condition holds, a repair or phase-I procedure is required.
review_flags: Supplied primal-dual locators concern interior-point or network methods, not simplex mode switching; a directly relevant source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility-based transitions between primal-simplex and dual-simplex pivot modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a basis \(B\) of the minimization problem \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), compute \(x_B=B^{-1}b\) and reduced costs \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^TB^{-T}c_B\). Given tolerances \(\tau_p,\tau_d\ge0\), call the basis primal feasible to tolerance when \(x_B\ge-\tau_p\mathbf 1\), and dual feasible to tolerance when \(\bar c_N\ge-\tau_d\mathbf 1\). Use primal simplex when the basis is primal feasible but not dual feasible, and use dual simplex when it is dual feasible but not primal feasible. If both feasibility conditions hold, declare tolerance-optimality. If neither condition holds, apply a basis-repair or phase-I procedure before selecting either mode. After every pivot, recompute residual tests and switch modes only when the corresponding maintained feasibility condition is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose primal simplex from a primal-feasible basis, dual simplex from a dual-feasible basis, and repair the basis first when neither feasibility condition holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Simplex Switching

children.title: Basis-Recovery Transition Interface
children.top_down_role: Transitions to repaired, reconstructed, or alternative starting bases.

children.title: Basis Restart Triggers
children.top_down_role: Solver conditions motivating a restart from an available basis state.

assumptions_latex: The linear program is maintained in standard form \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of row rank \(m\).
The current basis matrix \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is intended to support primal or dual simplex iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{restart}(B)=1\) holds exactly when at least one prescribed reliability test fails; a full basis restart is then requested instead of another pivot or local repair.

notation.meaning: Current basis index set and basis matrix.
Condition-number threshold, residual tolerance, and repair budget.
Number of consecutive unsuccessful local repairs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A solver-policy predicate separating recoverable basis defects from defects requiring complete reinitialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a nonsingular candidate basis \(B\), residual measures \(\rho_p=\lVert b-Ax\rVert\) and \(\rho_d=\lVert c-A^{\mathsf T}y-s\rVert\), and unsuccessful-repair count \(r\), define a restart trigger by
\[
\operatorname{restart}(B)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(B\text{ is singular}\bigr)\ \lor\ \bigl(\kappa(B)>\kappa_{\max}\bigr)\ \lor\ \bigl(\max\{\rho_p,\rho_d\}>\tau\bigr)\ \lor\ \bigl(r>r_{\max}\bigr).
\]
Here \(\kappa_{\max}>0\), \(\tau>0\), and \(r_{\max}\in\mathbb N\) are solver parameters. When the predicate is true, the solver abandons incremental basis recovery and invokes full basis reinitialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart the basis when it is singular, excessively ill-conditioned, persistently inaccurate, or has exhausted the permitted number of local repair attempts.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Restart Triggers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the statement assumes a nonsingular candidate basis while simultaneously testing whether that same basis is singular. The proposed disjunction and configurable thresholds are solver-specific policy choices with no cited source, so the exact predicate cannot be validated.

children.title: Basis Repair Transitions
children.top_down_role: Transitions using repaired or stabilized versions of an existing basis.

assumptions_latex: The linear program is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
A candidate basis index set \(\mathcal B\) has cardinality \(m\), but \(A_{\mathcal B}\) is singular, ill-conditioned, or inconsistent with the desired primal or dual status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the repair terminates successfully, the returned set \(\widehat{\mathcal B}\) has cardinality \(m\), \(A_{\widehat{\mathcal B}}\) is nonsingular, and its associated basic state passes the prescribed feasibility and residual tests.

notation.meaning: Current and repaired basis index sets.
Indices eligible to enter the repaired basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract local basis-repair interface; concrete solvers use different rank, stability, and feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \((A,b,c,\mathcal B,\mathcal C,\tau)\). Initialize \(\widehat{\mathcal B}\leftarrow\mathcal B\). While \(A_{\widehat{\mathcal B}}\) fails the rank, conditioning, residual, or requested primal-or-dual feasibility test at tolerance \(\tau\), choose a leaving index \(i\in\widehat{\mathcal B}\) implicated by the failed test and an entering index \(j\in\mathcal C\setminus\widehat{\mathcal B}\), then set
\[
\widehat{\mathcal B}\leftarrow(\widehat{\mathcal B}\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.
\]
Accept only exchanges that improve a prescribed lexicographic repair measure. Stop with the first accepted nonsingular basis passing all tests; if no admissible exchange exists or the repair budget is exhausted, output \(\mathrm{RESTART}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange suspect basic columns for eligible nonbasic columns until rank, stability, residual, and requested feasibility tests pass; otherwise request a complete restart.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Repair Transitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the transition leaf, but the leaving-index rule, entering-index rule, lexicographic repair measure, acceptance tests, and repair budget are unspecified solver policies. With no source, neither the procedure nor its successful-output guarantee is inspectable.

children.title: Full Basis Reinitialization
children.top_down_role: Transitions that replace the current basis with a newly constructed starting basis.

assumptions_latex: The linear program is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of row rank \(m\).
Incremental repair has failed or a restart condition has been declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful reinitialization returns a nonsingular basis \(\mathcal B_0\) and an associated state satisfying the selected simplex phase's acceptance tests; otherwise it returns a valid infeasibility or initialization-failure status.

notation.meaning: Artificial variables used by an auxiliary Phase-I problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract Phase-I reinitialization after local recovery is abandoned.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Discard the current factorization and construct an auxiliary Phase-I problem with artificial variables \(a\ge0\) and an evident nonsingular starting basis. Apply a finite anti-cycling simplex rule to minimize \(\theta=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}a\). If the Phase-I optimum satisfies \(\theta>0\), report primal infeasibility. If \(\theta=0\), pivot every positive-cost artificial basic variable out whenever a rank-preserving original column is available, delete redundant rows when necessary, and obtain an original-column basis \(\mathcal B_0\). Recompute the basis factorization and primal-dual residuals from the original data; accept \(\mathcal B_0\) only if the prescribed numerical tests pass, otherwise report initialization failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rebuild a basis through Phase I, remove artificial basic variables, recompute the factorization and residuals, and either accept the new basis or report failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Full Basis Reinitialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits full basis reinitialization, but the auxiliary Phase-I construction and artificial-variable removal policy depend on the formulation and implementation. No source supports the stated procedure, and the conclusion's reference to a valid infeasibility status is broader than the primal-infeasibility outcome described in the statement.

children.title: Interior-Point Crossover Paths
children.top_down_role: Simplex trajectories used to recover a basic solution from an interior-point output.

assumptions_latex: The primal-dual pair is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).

An interior-point method supplies \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) with small primal-dual residuals and complementarity, and \(\tau>0\) is the crossover tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On successful termination, crossover returns a basic primal-dual solution \((x^*,y^*,s^*,\mathcal B)\) satisfying the requested feasibility and optimality tolerances.

notation.meaning: Candidate basis selected from near-active and near-positive components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic primal-dual crossover from an approximate interior solution to a basic optimal solution.

source_refs.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \((A,b,c,\bar x,\bar y,\bar s,\tau)\). Rank variables using \(\bar x_j\), \(\bar s_j\), and complementarity, and select \(m\) linearly independent columns forming a candidate basis \(\mathcal B\). Recompute the corresponding basic primal and dual quantities. While primal infeasibility, dual infeasibility, or nonbasic reduced-cost violation exceeds \(\tau\), perform primal or dual simplex pivots, using a finite anti-cycling rule and updating \(\mathcal B\). Stop when
\[
\lVert Ax-b\rVert\le\tau,\qquad \lVert A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\rVert\le\tau,\qquad x\ge-\tau\mathbf1,\quad s\ge-\tau\mathbf1,
\]
and output the resulting basic primal-dual solution; report crossover failure if no acceptable basis can be formed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a candidate basis from the interior-point output, then use primal or dual simplex pivots to obtain a basic solution satisfying feasibility and optimality tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Crossover Paths

source_witnesses.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

children.title: Polynomial Pivot-Rule Problem
children.top_down_role: The open search for a uniform simplex rule with polynomial worst-case path length.

assumptions_latex: Input linear programs have rational data and encoding length \(L\), with \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables.
A pivot rule selects an adjacent improving basis using only polynomially computable information from the current basis and input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polynomial pivot-rule problem asks whether some uniform rule guarantees at most \(p(m,n,L)\) pivots on every feasible bounded rational linear program, for a fixed polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the rational input.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision formulation of the open deterministic polynomial pivot-rule question in the rational bit model.

source_refs.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57
4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible bounded rational linear program with dimensions \((m,n)\) and binary encoding length \(L\), consider the directed graph of feasible bases whose arcs are objective-improving simplex pivots. The problem is to construct one deterministic, uniformly specified pivot rule and a polynomial \(p\) such that, from every permitted initial feasible basis, the rule reaches an optimal basis after at most \(p(m,n,L)\) pivots. Each pivot choice and update must also be computable in time polynomial in the current input representation. Exponential lower bounds for particular classical rules do not settle whether such a different uniform polynomial rule exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Does one deterministic simplex pivot rule reach an optimum in polynomially many pivots, measured in dimensions and rational input length, on every bounded feasible instance?
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Pivot-Rule Problem

source_witnesses.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57
4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is an appropriate kind for this open problem, but the cited older textbook sections do not establish its status as of the retrieval date. The restriction to strictly objective-improving arcs also needs authoritative clarification because degenerate simplex paths may require pivots with no strict objective improvement.

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Simplex Problem
children.top_down_role: The open boundary requiring structurally polynomial pivot and arithmetic work.

assumptions_latex: The linear program has rational data, \(m\) constraints, and \(n\) variables.
Arithmetic operations and comparisons are performed on numbers whose encoding lengths remain polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strongly polynomial simplex problem asks for a pivot algorithm using at most \(p(m,n)\) arithmetic operations and pivots, with intermediate encoding lengths polynomially bounded in the input length.

notation.meaning: Polynomial independent of coefficient magnitudes and input encoding length.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-polynomiality requires dimension-only operation bounds and controlled intermediate number sizes.

source_refs.locator: Polynomial and Strongly Polynomial Algorithms p. 58
EIGHT: COMPLEXITY OF THE SIMPLEX ALGORITHM AND POLYNOMIAL-TIME ALGORITHMS p. 393

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The required object is a uniform simplex-type algorithm for rational linear programming and a polynomial \(p\) such that every instance with dimensions \((m,n)\) is solved using at most \(p(m,n)\) pivots and arithmetic operations, independently of the binary encoding length \(L\) and the magnitudes of the coefficients. In addition, every intermediate rational number must have encoding length bounded by a polynomial in \(L\), so that the arithmetic-operation bound corresponds to polynomial bit complexity. A pivot bound polynomial in \((m,n,L)\) alone is insufficient: it establishes at most weak polynomiality, not strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Can a simplex-type method use only dimension-polynomially many pivots and arithmetic operations, independent of coefficient magnitudes, while keeping all intermediate numbers polynomially encoded?
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Simplex Problem

source_witnesses.locator: Polynomial and Strongly Polynomial Algorithms p. 58
EIGHT: COMPLEXITY OF THE SIMPLEX ALGORITHM AND POLYNOMIAL-TIME ALGORITHMS p. 393

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the leaf, and the stated distinction between dimension-only arithmetic bounds and bit-size control is mathematically standard. Because the record presents this as a currently open simplex problem, however, the older textbook locators are insufficient to verify current status and the precise simplex-type restriction.

children.title: Randomized Polynomial Pivot Problem
children.top_down_role: The boundary between established randomized regimes and polynomial expected pivot complexity.

assumptions_latex: Input linear programs have rational data, dimensions \((m,n)\), encoding length \(L\), and a permitted initial feasible basis.
At each basis, the pivot rule may use internal randomness but must select an admissible adjacent pivot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem asks whether a uniform randomized rule can guarantee \(\mathbb E[T]\le p(m,n,L)\) for every input, or the stronger bound \(\mathbb E[T]\le p(m,n)\), where \(T\) is the number of pivots to optimality.

notation.meaning: Random number of pivots until an optimal basis is reached.
Expectation over the rule's internal randomness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected pivot complexity under internal randomization, distinguished from distributional average-case analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each feasible bounded rational linear program and initial feasible basis, let \(T\) be the stopping time at which a randomized local pivot rule first reaches an optimal basis. The polynomial expected-pivot question seeks one uniform rule and a polynomial \(p\) satisfying
\[
\mathbb E[T]\le p(m,n,L)
\]
for every fixed input, where the expectation is solely over the rule's internal random choices. The strongly polynomial variant replaces the right-hand side by \(p(m,n)\) and also requires polynomially bounded arithmetic work and intermediate encoding lengths. A polynomial expectation under a chosen probability distribution on inputs does not by itself satisfy this worst-input guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Is there a randomized local pivot rule whose expected number of pivots is polynomial for every fixed input, rather than merely on average over an input distribution?
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Polynomial Pivot Problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct role, and the distinction between expectation over internal randomness and average case over inputs is coherent. No citation supports the exact worst-input randomized formulation, its stronger dimension-only variant, or their current open status.

children.title: Diameter-to-Pivot-Rule Problem
children.top_down_role: The problem of converting global short-path information into a uniform local pivot policy.

assumptions_latex: For a polyhedron \(P\), let \(G(P)\) be its vertex-edge graph and let \(D(P)\) be the maximum shortest-path distance between two vertices.
A simplex pivot policy must choose its next adjacent vertex from information computable at the current state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conversion problem asks whether polynomial bounds on \(D(P)\) can be made algorithmic through a uniform local rule whose monotone path to an optimum has polynomial length.

notation.meaning: Vertex-edge graph of the feasible polyhedron.
Undirected graph diameter of the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates global undirected short paths from locally discoverable objective-monotone simplex paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound \(D(P)\le q(m,n)\) asserts that any two vertices of \(P\) are joined by some undirected edge path of length at most \(q(m,n)\). The diameter-to-pivot-rule problem asks for conditions or a construction converting such global existence into a uniform pivot policy that, for every linear objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) and starting vertex, selects locally available nonworsening or improving edges and reaches an optimal vertex in polynomially many pivots. The logical gap is that a shortest undirected path may use objective-decreasing edges, may depend on the unknown destination, and need not be identifiable from local basis information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short undirected path between vertices need not be objective-monotone or locally discoverable; the problem is to convert global diameter bounds into a uniform efficient pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Diameter-to-Pivot-Rule Problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the container, but no source supports this exact conversion problem. In particular, the permitted use of nonworsening versus strictly improving edges, the treatment of degeneracy, and the relationship among undirected diameter, monotone diameter, and a locally computable pivot rule require an authoritative formulation.

children.title: Worst-Case versus Practice Explanation Problem
children.top_down_role: The search for predictive structural, probabilistic, and implementation-sensitive explanations of observed efficiency.

assumptions_latex: A family of simplex implementations is fixed, including pivot selection, presolve, scaling, degeneracy handling, numerical tolerances, and basis updates.
An instance model or empirically specified population \(\mathcal D\) and measurable work variable \(T(I)\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A satisfactory explanation supplies verifiable conditions and bounds predicting the distribution of \(T(I)\) under \(I\sim\mathcal D\), while remaining consistent with exponential worst-case families outside those conditions.

notation.meaning: Measured pivot count or computational work on instance I.
Random instance drawn from the specified population.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the explanatory gap between exponential constructions and typical solver behavior.

source_refs.locator: Polynomial Versus Exponential, Worst Case Versus Average Case p. 50
4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(I)\) denote the pivot count or arithmetic work of a fully specified simplex implementation on instance \(I\). The explanation problem is to identify checkable structural assumptions or a reproducible distribution \(\mathcal D\) for which quantitative predictions such as
\[
\Pr_{I\sim\mathcal D}\{T(I)>t\}\le g(t,m,n)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[T(I)]\le p(m,n)
\]
can be established and validated. The model must expose the effects of degeneracy, conditioning, sparsity, presolve, scaling, pivot pricing, and numerical basis maintenance. It must also permit adversarial families with exponential \(T(I)\); average or typical efficiency does not contradict exponential worst-case complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The problem is to predict practical simplex work from explicit instance structure, probability models, and implementation choices while remaining compatible with exponential worst-case examples.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case versus Practice Explanation Problem

source_witnesses.locator: Polynomial Versus Exponential, Worst Case Versus Average Case p. 50
4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is a reasonable role for this methodological explanation problem. The supplied textbook locators concern worst-case and average-case complexity generally, but they do not inspectably support the record's stronger requirement to model all listed implementation features or the proposed tail-bound and expectation criteria. A source specifically addressing empirical, probabilistic, or implementation-sensitive simplex behavior is required.
